newsitem.title: USA: FBI warned 6 lawmakers about China money - Post.
newsitem.headline: FBI warned 6 lawmakers about China money - Post.

text.p: The FBI warned six members of Congress last year that they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign contributions from foreign corporations, the Washington Post reported on Sunday.
Quoting U.S. government officials, the newspaper said the unusual warnings were based on "specific and credible" intelligence information.

Individual classified briefings delivered to the lawmakers included this statement: "We have reason to believe that the government of China may try to make contributions to members of Congress through Asian donors," the Post said in Sunday editions.
Sen. Dianne Feinstein, a California Democrat, was the only lawmaker identified in the story. The newspaper said the identities of the others could not be confirmed.

The paper quoted a spokesman for Feinstein as saying she received the FBI briefing in June and decided on Friday to return $12,000 in campaign contributions from donors associated with Indonesia's Lippo Group, a financial conglomerate with extensive dealings in China.

Officials told the paper a Justice Department task force investigating allegations of improper fund raising has found no evidence that Feinstein or other lawmakers knowingly received illegal payments from the Chinese government.
But investigators did find "conclusive evidence" that Chinese government funds were funnelled into the United States last year, the newspaper said.

It said it remained uncertain whether any of the money ended up in presidential or congressional campaign coffers. Such contributions would violate federal law, which prohibits foreign individuals, corporations or governments from funding U.S. campaigns.

A Justice Department review of foreign intelligence information showed that in early 1995, Chinese representatives developed a plan to spend nearly $2 million to buy influence not only in Congress but also within the Clinton administration, according to the Post report.
It quoted a spokesman for the Chinese embassy categorically denying allegations that Beijing has attempted to influence U.S. elections.
The Post said Justice Department officials informed National Security Council staff workers about the matter last June, but they were not given the names of the lawmakers targeted by China.

A White House official told the paper that neither President Bill Clinton nor senior policymakers were briefed on the matter. A senior White House official was quoted as saying the White House was unaware of alleged Chinese efforts to funnel money into presidential campaigns until reading news accounts last month.

Pressure is building on Attorney General Janet Reno for an independent investigation into the Democratic fund-raising controversy, although she has so far refused to seek the appointment of an independent counsel.
